summary: This work demonstrates vacuum-limited trapping lifetimes exceeding 7000 s (∼2 hours) for single $^{88}$Sr atoms in optical tweezers using a simple cryogenic design with a 4 K cold tip, while maintaining full optical access without complex in-vacuum windows. The apparatus achieves high vacuum pressure ($\sim 2.5 \times 10^{-12}$ mbar) through material selection (grade 2 titanium), bakeout procedures, and hydrogen cryopumping, without the thermal load constraints that limit scaling in conventional 4 K platforms.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are scaling toward 10,000+ qubits, but existing platforms face a tradeoff between optical accessibility and atom storage lifetime due to background gas collisions and the complexity of cryogenic enclosures that restrict optical access. Extending trapping lifetimes while preserving optical access is essential for sorting large defect-free arrays and enabling scaled quantum processors.
method: A bakeable UHV chamber constructed primarily from grade 2 titanium (superior hydrogen outgassing characteristics) was coupled to a commercial closed-cycle cryostat (ColdEdge Stinger) cooling a cold tip to 4 K approximately 30 cm from the tweezer array. Single $^{88}$Sr atoms in a $16 \times 16$ optical tweezer array (spacing 4 µm, depth ∼220 µK) were held under various cooling protocols (continuous/pulsed Sisyphus cooling, pulsed sideband cooling) to measure survival probability versus hold time and distinguish loss mechanisms.
result: With pulsed Sisyphus and sideband cooling, lifetimes exceed 7000 s; without cooling, lifetimes reach several hundred seconds even at room temperature. Deliberately heating the cold tip to 30 K induces a pressure spike from hydrogen desorption, confirming the cold tip acts as a cryopump. Lifetime increases monotonically with tweezer trap depth and decreases with oven temperature, while remaining independent of tweezer optical power (up to the tested range), demonstrating compatibility with scaling to large arrays without thermal load degradation of the cryogenic system.
